## Introduction: a centered Gaussian quantity

Let $X\sim N_d(0,I_d)$ and let $g:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$ be weakly differentiable. Write $\partial_i=\partial/\partial x_i$ and use the Jacobian convention

$$
(\nabla g)_{ij}=\partial_j g_i,
\qquad
\operatorname{div}g=\sum_{i=1}^d\partial_i g_i.
$$

Throughout, assume Gaussian square integrability:

$$
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|g(X)\|_2^2+\|\nabla g(X)\|_F^2\right]<\infty.
$$

First-order Stein's lemma is Gaussian integration by parts, applied to each scalar component $g_j$:

$$
\mathbb{E}[X_i g_j(X)]
=\mathbb{E}[\partial_i g_j(X)],
\qquad 1\leq i,j\leq d.
$$

Taking $i=j$ and summing the diagonal entries gives

$$
\mathbb{E}[X^\top g(X)]
=\sum_{i=1}^d\mathbb{E}[X_i g_i(X)]
=\sum_{i=1}^d\mathbb{E}[\partial_i g_i(X)]
=\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{div}g(X)].
$$

Thus the random variable

$$
\varepsilon(X)=X^\top g(X)-\operatorname{div}g(X)
$$

has $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon(X)]=0$. The next question is how much it fluctuates around zero.

## Statement: its variance is explicit

Under the assumptions above, the second-order Stein identity states[^bellec-zhang]

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon(X))
=\mathbb{E}\|g(X)\|_2^2
+\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[(\nabla g(X))^2\right].
\tag{1}
$$

The square inside the trace is **matrix multiplication**:

$$
\operatorname{Tr}[(\nabla g)^2]
=\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{j=1}^d
(\partial_j g_i)(\partial_i g_j).
$$

This term can be negative. It equals $\|\nabla g\|_F^2$ when the Jacobian is symmetric.

## Motivation: uncertainty in SURE

Suppose $Y=\mu+X$, with unknown $\mu\in\mathbb{R}^d$, and consider an estimator $\widehat\mu(Y)$ satisfying the corresponding regularity conditions. Stein's unbiased risk estimate is

$$
\operatorname{SURE}(Y)
=\|\widehat\mu(Y)-Y\|_2^2
+2\operatorname{div}\widehat\mu(Y)-d.
$$

First-order Stein gives $\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{SURE}]=\mathbb{E}[L]$, where $L=\|\widehat\mu(Y)-\mu\|_2^2$ is the realized squared loss. Second-order Stein addresses the accuracy of SURE itself. In fact, setting

$$
h_\mu(x)=x+2\{\widehat\mu(\mu+x)-(\mu+x)\}
$$

gives $L-\operatorname{SURE}=X^\top h_\mu(X)-\operatorname{div}h_\mu(X)$. Applying (1) to $h_\mu$ computes $\mathbb{E}[(\operatorname{SURE}-L)^2]$ exactly; no limit in $d$ is required.

## Derivation

### 1. Insert a scalar test function

Let $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ be weakly differentiable with $\mathbb{E}[f(X)^2+\|\nabla f(X)\|_2^2]<\infty$. Applying first-order Stein to each product $f g_i$, then using the product rule, yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[f(X)\varepsilon(X)]
&=\sum_{i=1}^d
\left\{\mathbb{E}[X_i f(X)g_i(X)]
-\mathbb{E}[f(X)\partial_i g_i(X)]\right\}\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^d
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\partial_i(fg_i)(X)-f(X)\partial_i g_i(X)\right]\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^d\mathbb{E}[g_i(X)\partial_i f(X)]\\
&=\mathbb{E}[g(X)^\top\nabla f(X)].
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
$$

The derivative of $g_i$ cancels with the divergence correction. This identity turns multiplication by $\varepsilon$ into differentiation of the test function.

### 2. Choose the test function $f=\varepsilon$

For this calculation, first assume $g$ is smooth and its derivatives have at most polynomial growth. This justifies differentiating $\varepsilon$; we remove the extra smoothness below. All functions in the following displays are evaluated at $X$.

For each $i$,

$$
\partial_i\varepsilon
=g_i
+\sum_{j=1}^d X_j\partial_i g_j
-\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_i\partial_j g_j.
$$

Substitute this expression into (3):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^2]
&=\sum_{i=1}^d\mathbb{E}[g_i\partial_i\varepsilon]\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^d\mathbb{E}[g_i^2]
+\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{j=1}^d
\mathbb{E}[X_j g_i\partial_i g_j]\\
&\qquad
-\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{j=1}^d
\mathbb{E}[g_i\partial_i\partial_j g_j].
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
$$

Apply first-order Stein again, now in coordinate $j$, to the middle term:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X_j g_i\partial_i g_j]
&=\mathbb{E}[\partial_j(g_i\partial_i g_j)]\\
&=\mathbb{E}[(\partial_j g_i)(\partial_i g_j)]
+\mathbb{E}[g_i\partial_j\partial_i g_j].
\end{aligned}
$$

Because mixed partial derivatives commute, the second-derivative terms cancel in (4). Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^2]
&=\sum_{i=1}^d\mathbb{E}[g_i^2]
+\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{j=1}^d
\mathbb{E}[(\partial_j g_i)(\partial_i g_j)]\\
&=\mathbb{E}\|g(X)\|_2^2
+\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}[(\nabla g(X))^2].
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon]=0$, this proves (1).


## A quick check

Take $g(x)=x$. Then $\varepsilon(X)=\|X\|_2^2-d$, and

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\|X\|_2^2-d)
=\mathbb{E}\|X\|_2^2+\operatorname{Tr}(I_d^2)
=d+d=2d,
$$

the familiar variance of a $\chi_d^2$ variable.

[^bellec-zhang]: Bellec, P. C., and Zhang, C.-H. (2021). *Second-order Stein: SURE for SURE and other applications in high-dimensional inference*. **The Annals of Statistics**, 49(4), 1864--1903. [doi:10.1214/20-AOS2005](https://doi.org/10.1214/20-AOS2005). See Theorem 2.1 for the identity and Section 3.1 for SURE. [Open-access preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.04121).
